messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo was 22 when he came for help, a single HVAC technician who had built his life around early starts, roof work, compressor repairs, and the hard physical routines that made sense to him. The event that changed everything had happened on an ordinary job site in late summer, during a service call in a cramped apartment complex where the hallway units were humming and the air outside was heavy and still. While moving equipment, Mateo had made a mistake that resulted in another man being seriously injured. He described the moment with a kind of stunned precision, as if replaying the sequence might somehow produce a different ending: the sudden movement, the impact, the shock of seeing the other person go down, and the smell that rose in the aftermath, metallic and sharp, which he could still catch in his mind without warning. From that day on, the memory never felt like something safely in the past. He said it felt alien, as though it belonged to somebody else’s life, yet it would force its way into his mind when he was trying to work, drive, or fall asleep, and when it came it often arrived with that same smell attached.

In the weeks after the injury, Mateo became obsessed with figuring out exactly where his judgment had failed and how one small decision had snowballed into catastrophe. He went over the details again and again, convinced he had to find the point at which he should have done more, stopped sooner, noticed faster. What sat underneath that replaying was a set of harsh conclusions about himself: that his body could not be trusted anymore, that the person he had become was unrecognisable to him, and that he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. Those beliefs began to shape what he did next. He started avoiding anything he imagined could turn stressful, cutting short conversations, declining extra work, and turning down jobs that felt unpredictable. He would not look at dates linked to the incident and became uneasy as anniversaries approached, as if the calendar itself were a warning. The more he tried to control his life by narrowing it, the more certain he became that he could not rely on himself, because if he had truly been competent, the injury would not have happened. His shrinking world fed the self-condemnation, and the self-condemnation made his avoidance feel necessary.

That avoidance came with its own costs. Mateo had once been the kind of technician who could move between noisy mechanical rooms, crowded stairwells, and unfamiliar buildings without much thought, but now he only felt safe in a very limited number of places, mainly his bedroom, his truck, and a corner of his mother’s kitchen where he knew exactly what every sound meant. At work, even the everyday silence between machines could put him on edge; if a unit shut off and the hallway went still, he would tense before he could stop himself, certain that something dangerous was about to happen. When that happened, his body reacted strongly and immediately, with a pounding heart, a tight chest, and a jolt of dread that seemed to confirm his fear that something was wrong with him. Those physical surges made the old scene intrude more forcefully, and once the memory came in, it brought the threat with it: the apartment hallway, the smell, the sense that disaster could break open again at any moment. He would then pull back further, skipping calls he could have managed and asking coworkers to take over situations that felt too exposed or too loud. Over time, his efforts to stay safe made the world feel more dangerous, not less, because every restricted route and every quiet room taught him that only a few places could contain the alarm.

By the time he entered treatment, Mateo had lost confidence in his own body and in the version of himself who used to trust it. He was still showing up to work, but he was doing so with constant monitoring, measuring his reactions, scanning for silence, and bracing for the next unwanted image. He had not been able to bring himself to face the anniversary without dread, and what finally pushed him to seek help was the fear that his life was getting smaller around the injury he caused. He wanted to stop living as though every stressful moment might bring the whole scene back, and he was most afraid that his guilt had already changed him into someone he could never become again.
